title: Campus notifications: SMS, push and email at scale

authoring.author: Parikshaa content team
authoring.originality: Written for Parikshaa: our own notification service design case, examples, code, quiz and explanations; no text from any site, book or course.

scenario: The university's apps (results, fees, hostel, exams) all send messages to students by SMS, push and email. On result day one call asks to notify **12 lakh students**, while login OTPs must still arrive within seconds. SMS providers accept only a limited rate and sometimes fail. Design a shared notification service.

clarifying_questions.a: Transactional (OTP, fee receipt: urgent, one user) and bulk (result published, exam notice: many users, minutes are fine).
The SMS provider allows 500 messages per second per account; push and email providers allow far more.
Of bulk messages per channel, yes; of OTPs, no.
A duplicate OTP or fee SMS confuses people and costs money: avoid duplicates; at-least-once internally is fine if delivery is deduplicated.
Yes: per message status (queued, sent, delivered, failed) and per campaign counts.
Yes: senders pass a template id and variables; the service renders text per channel and language.

functional: Accept a notification for one user or a campaign for a list or segment of users
Render per channel and language from templates
Deliver through providers with retries and fallbacks
Report status per message and per campaign

non_functional.name: OTP latency
non_functional.target: p99 under 5 seconds from request to provider, even during a bulk campaign

non_functional.name: Bulk throughput
non_functional.target: 12 lakh SMS within one hour, within the provider's 500 per second

non_functional.name: Duplicates
non_functional.target: at most one delivery per (message, channel)

non_functional.name: Durability
non_functional.target: an accepted notification is never silently lost

estimates.question: At 500 SMS per second, how many minutes does a 12-lakh SMS campaign take?
estimates.working: 12,00,000 / 500 = 2,400 s = 40 minutes: the provider limit, not our servers, sets the pace.

estimates.question: If OTPs average 20 per second, what share of the 500 per second SMS budget must be reserved for them, in percent?
estimates.working: 20 / 500 = 4%; reserving about 10% gives headroom for OTP spikes.

estimates.question: Status records per year if 3 crore messages are sent and each has about 3 status updates, in crore rows?
estimates.working: 3 crore × 3 = 9 crore rows a year: partition by month and archive old ones.

estimates.question: Size of the backlog when a whole 12-lakh campaign is queued at 1 KB per message, in GB?
estimates.working: 12,00,000 × 1 KB = 1.2 GB: easily held by a durable queue.

expected_components.name: Notification API with idempotency keys
expected_components.why: Senders retry; the same key must not create a second message.

expected_components.name: Campaign fan-out workers
expected_components.why: Expand a segment into per-user messages in batches, instead of the caller sending 12 lakh requests.

expected_components.name: Separate priority queues (transactional vs bulk) per channel
expected_components.why: A bulk backlog must never delay an OTP.

expected_components.name: Per-provider rate limiter (token bucket)
expected_components.why: Keeps sending within 500 per second with a reserved share for OTPs.

expected_components.name: Channel senders with retry, backoff and fallback
expected_components.why: Provider errors are retried with growing delays; a failed push can fall back to SMS for important messages.

expected_components.name: Preference and opt-out store
expected_components.why: Checked at fan-out and again just before sending.

expected_components.name: Template service
expected_components.why: Renders text per channel and language from versioned templates.

expected_components.name: Status store and provider webhooks
expected_components.why: Records queued, sent, delivered and failed; aggregates campaign counts.

expected_components.name: Dead-letter queue
expected_components.why: Messages that keep failing are parked for inspection instead of retried forever.

api: POST /notifications {user_id, template_id, vars, channels, priority, idempotency_key} → 202 {message_id}
POST /campaigns {segment | user_ids_file, template_id, vars, channels, send_at?} → 202 {campaign_id}
data_model: messages(message_id, idempotency_key UNIQUE, user_id, template_id, vars, priority, campaign_id, created_at); deliveries(message_id, channel, attempt, status, provider_msg_id UNIQUE, updated_at) partitioned by month; preferences(user_id, channel, bulk_opt_out); campaigns(campaign_id, segment, template_id, counts).

diagram.alt: Senders call the notification API; campaigns go to fan-out workers that read preferences and enqueue per-user messages into bulk queues; single messages go to transactional queues; channel senders read both queues through a rate limiter that reserves capacity for transactional traffic, call SMS, push and email providers, and write statuses; provider webhooks update statuses; failures go to a dead-letter queue.

deep_dives.topic: OTPs never wait behind a campaign
deep_dives.body: Each channel has two queues: transactional and bulk. The SMS sender takes tokens from one 500 per second bucket, but **reserves** a share (say 50 per second) that only transactional messages may use, and always drains the transactional queue first. A 40-minute campaign backlog therefore never adds latency to an OTP; at worst it slows the campaign slightly.

deep_dives.topic: At-least-once inside, at-most-once to the user
deep_dives.body: Queues redeliver messages after a crash, so a sender may see the same delivery twice. Before calling the provider it records `(message_id, channel)` as SENDING with a unique constraint; a second worker finds it and skips. Providers that accept a client reference get `message_id` as that reference, so even a retry after a timeout is deduplicated on their side. Status webhooks are keyed by `provider_msg_id` and are idempotent.

Temporary provider errors (timeouts, 5xx, throttling) are retried with exponential backoff and jitter: 2 s, 4 s, 8 s ... up to a limit, so a provider outage is not hammered by synchronized retries. Permanent errors (invalid number) stop at once. After the last retry the message goes to a dead-letter queue. For important messages, a failed push falls back to SMS.

trade_offs: Separate queues and a reserved token share add moving parts but are the only reliable way to keep OTPs fast during bulk sends.
Deduplicating with a unique (message, channel) record costs one write per delivery but prevents double SMS charges and confused users.
Fan-out in the service (not the caller) concentrates load in one place but lets the service batch, apply preferences and pace sends.
failure_modes: The SMS provider is down: messages wait in queues and retry with backoff; important ones fall back to push or a second provider.
A sender worker crashes mid-send: the queue redelivers; the dedupe record prevents a second SMS.
A bad template ships: rendering fails for every message, which go to dead letters; fix the template and replay.
The status store is slow: senders buffer status updates; delivery itself continues.

rubric.criterion: Separates transactional and bulk traffic and asks about provider limits, opt-outs and duplicates.
Estimates campaign duration, OTP share, status volume and backlog, and uses them.
Keeps OTP latency low during bulk sends: separate queues and reserved rate.
At-least-once internally with deduplication, retries with backoff, fallbacks and dead letters.
Clear API, fan-out, preferences, templates and status design.
Trade-offs and failure handling explained (AI feedback, advice only).

concept_checks.stem: A 12-lakh SMS campaign is queued at 10:00 and an OTP request arrives at 10:01. What keeps the OTP fast?
options: A separate transactional queue drained first, with reserved send rate
concept_checks.explanation: Priority isolation: separate queue plus reserved tokens.

concept_checks.stem: At 500 SMS per second, roughly how long does 12 lakh SMS take?
A worker crashes after calling the SMS provider but before acknowledging the queue. What prevents a duplicate SMS when the message is redelivered?
options: A unique (message_id, channel) send record and the provider's client reference
concept_checks.explanation: Idempotent sending: record the attempt and pass a client reference.

concept_checks.stem: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
options: So many failed messages do not retry in lockstep and hit the provider at the same instant

revision_card.front: Notification service: how do OTPs stay fast during a bulk campaign, and how are duplicates avoided?
revision_card.back: Separate transactional and bulk queues per channel; rate limiter with a reserved share for transactional, drained first. Duplicates: idempotency key at the API, unique (message, channel) send record, provider client reference, idempotent webhooks. Retries with exponential backoff + jitter, dead letters.
